title: South Asian Filmmakers Are Building Their Own Pipeline from Cannes to Tribeca. Here Is How.
excerpt: Box Office Guru Media's initiative connects diaspora creatives with studios, agencies, and distributors through structured pitch sessions and industry networking.
body:
Box Office Guru Media has wrapped its "South Asians at Cannes" initiative at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival and officially launched "South Asians at Tribeca," extending a growing network that is quietly reshaping how diaspora filmmakers access Hollywood's corridors of power.

The initiative, which ran parallel to the main festival and the Marché du Film, brought together filmmakers, studio executives, producers, and artists from across the South Asian diaspora and the broader international film community. BOGM collaborated with RecDek, South Stack Studios, Lotus Visual Productions, RASA Film Group, and Khan & Kumar Media to host events including a Bollywood Happy Hour activation, a Women in Film breakfast, and a series of strategic pitch sessions at The Impact Lounge.

## From Cannes to Tribeca

The programming was not limited to panels. BOGM's One-on-One Program — a cornerstone of its Industry Days initiative since 2004 — connected festival filmmakers directly with leading professionals from studios, production companies, distribution houses, and talent agencies through focused 15-minute meetings. For South Asian filmmakers who have historically struggled to get those meetings through conventional channels, the format offers something rare: direct, structured access.

At Cannes, BOGM also announced the launch of a new vertical production arm focused on developing and producing short-form vertical content designed for next-generation digital platforms. The move acknowledges a shift that diaspora audiences are already living — consuming entertainment on phones, in vertical format, across platforms that traditional studios have been slow to address.

## Tribeca and Beyond

Building on the Cannes momentum, BOGM is preparing a slate of activations for the 2026 Tribeca Festival under the "South Asians at Tribeca" banner. Partners include the Sundaram Tagore Gallery, Epicenter, the Islamic Scholarship Fund, and the South Asian House. Panel topics announced so far include "Animating the Future: South Asians in Visual Arts," "Interactive Worlds: Gaming as the Next Frontier for South Asian Storytelling," and "The Hybrid Release: Combining Alternative & Traditional Distribution in 2026."

The panels reflect a community that is no longer content with being represented on screen alone. South Asian creatives are now pushing into animation, gaming, and hybrid distribution — areas where the gatekeeping has historically been even more rigid than in live-action cinema.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

The Indian and broader South Asian diaspora has long been Hollywood's most reliable audience for crossover content. NRI families filled theatres for everything from *Slumdog Millionaire* to *RRR* to *Monkey Man*. But behind the camera, South Asian representation in decision-making roles — at studios, agencies, and distribution companies — has lagged far behind what the audience numbers would suggest.

Initiatives like BOGM's are designed to close that gap, not through advocacy alone but through the mechanics of the industry itself: pitch sessions, co-production deals, distribution partnerships, and talent pipelines. The One-on-One format, running since 2004, has already helped launch careers that now span feature films, streaming series, and festival circuits.

The 2026 edition of these efforts comes at a moment when South Asian stories are gaining unprecedented visibility globally. Netflix's Telugu and Tamil expansion, Amazon's investment in Indian originals, and the international success of films like *Karuppu* have created a market appetite that these networking events are positioned to feed.

For the South Asian filmmaker in New York, Los Angeles, or London who has the script but not the meeting, Tribeca may offer exactly the door that Cannes opened.
